lessons.title: A bounded problem
lessons.subtitle: Week 14: Planning your practical project
lessons.body:
A practical project should address a specific task for a defined audience. Narrow scope makes it easier to evaluate whether the result is useful.

Offline practice: Choose an AI-learning demonstration based on your own interests; write the audience and one measurable task. Write your reasoning before looking at the quiz answers. Record one limitation or uncertainty. You can use paper or local notes; an online AI tool is optional.

Recap: explain yesterday’s key idea from memory, then check your notes. After a break, start with this recap and the first small step of today’s activity.

Complete all three quiz questions before moving on.
takeaways: A practical project should address a specific task for a defined audience. Narrow scope makes it easier to evaluate whether the result is useful.
Apply the idea through the offline activity.
Keep reasoning, evidence, and limitations with your artifact.
lessons.sourceName: UNESCO guidance on responsible AI in education

questions.prompt: Which statement best explains “A bounded problem”?
options: The human learner never needs to check the result.
Every task requires training a new model.
A practical project should address a specific task for a defined audience. Narrow scope makes it easier to evaluate whether the result is useful.
A polished AI answer is enough evidence that every claim is correct.
questions.explanation: A practical project should address a specific task for a defined audience. Narrow scope makes it easier to evaluate whether the result is useful.

questions.prompt: For the activity “Choose an AI-learning demonstration based on your own interests; write the audience and one measurable task.”, which approach demonstrates learning?
options: Treat an unverified generated response as final evidence.

Complete the activity, explain your reasoning, and record a limitation.
Share someone else’s private information to make the example realistic.
questions.explanation: The activity asks you to apply this lesson. A written explanation and limitation make your understanding reviewable; a copied result alone does not.

questions.prompt: You return to the “A bounded problem” lesson after a break without internet. What can you do next?
options: Wait until you can buy a paid AI subscription.
Delete your previous work and start the whole course again.
Recall the key idea, check saved notes, and complete the offline activity.
Assume a cloud assistant will respond without a connection.
questions.explanation: The lesson and practice do not require an online tool. Retrieval and a small saved activity help you resume.

lessons.title: Permitted inputs
lessons.subtitle: Week 14: Planning your practical project
lessons.body:
Use inputs you are allowed to use and keep private information out of the project. A publicly visible item is not automatically free to redistribute.

lessons.title: Project schedule
lessons.subtitle: Week 14: Planning your practical project
lessons.body:
A small project schedule allocates time to preparation, drafting, checking, and revision. Keep a fallback for lost connectivity and unexpected delays.

Offline practice: Create a five-session schedule with one check or artifact per session. Write your reasoning before looking at the quiz answers. Record one limitation or uncertainty. You can use paper or local notes; an online AI tool is optional.

Recap: explain yesterday’s key idea from memory, then check your notes. After a break, start with this recap and the first small step of today’s activity.

Complete all three quiz questions before moving on.

Keep reasoning, evidence, and limitations with your artifact.

lessons.title: Project proposal
lessons.subtitle: Week 14: Planning your practical project
lessons.body:
A proposal combines the problem, audience, inputs, method, review plan, and expected artifact. It describes an intention, not proven impact.

Offline practice: Save a one-page proposal and ask a peer to identify unclear steps if a peer is available. Write your reasoning before looking at the quiz answers. Record one limitation or uncertainty. You can use paper or local notes; an online AI tool is optional.

Recap: explain yesterday’s key idea from memory, then check your notes. After a break, start with this recap and the first small step of today’s activity.

Complete all three quiz questions before moving on.

Weekly completion task: save this week’s practice artifact. Confirm four steps: explain a key idea (recap); complete the practice activity (practice); record what you would verify and where (plan); show your artifact and explain one improvement (demonstrate).
takeaways: A proposal combines the problem, audience, inputs, method, review plan, and expected artifact. It describes an intention, not proven impact.
Apply the idea through the offline activity.
Keep reasoning, evidence, and limitations with your artifact.
